Pancho is a Mexican-race avocado bred for cold hardiness, part of the small group of dooryard cultivars (alongside Joey, Lila, and Fantastic) that Gulf Coast and Texas growers rely on for in-ground avocado production outside the traditional Florida and California growing regions. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and rich in flavor with the anise-scented foliage typical of the Mexican race. Because avocados bear more reliably with cross-pollination between a Type A and Type B flowering cultivar, plant Pancho alongside a complementary flowering-type variety where space allows. Established trees tolerate brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit with only minor damage, though young trees need protection their first two or three winters before developing full cold tolerance.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in Texas

Fantastic is a Mexican-race avocado selected for cold hardiness and dependable fruiting, grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists alongside sister selections like Joey and Lila as part of the small pool of avocado cultivars that can be planted in-ground north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium with thin, edible-adjacent skin typical of Mexican-race avocados and rich, high-oil-content flesh with a pronounced anise note in the foliage and fruit. Fruit set improves with a complementary Type A or Type B flowering cultivar planted nearby. Mature, well-established trees can shrug off brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit, though reliable fruiting still depends on avoiding a hard freeze during bloom.

Wilma is one of the Mexican-race cold-hardy avocado selections identified and propagated by Texas dooryard growers for in-ground planting where standard Florida and California avocado varieties would not survive winter. Fruit is small to medium, dark-skinned, and rich-flavored with the characteristic anise-scented leaves of the Mexican race, ripening over a late-summer to fall window typical of these cold-hardy types. Plant with a complementary flowering-type cultivar nearby for the best fruit set, since cross-pollination between Type A and Type B avocados generally improves yield over a single tree alone. Mature trees tolerate brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit; young trees remain the most vulnerable and should be protected through at least their first two winters.

Opal is a Mexican-race cold-hardy avocado cultivar grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists as part of the small group of named selections that make in-ground avocado growing possible north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and richly flavored, with the anise-scented foliage characteristic of Mexican-race avocados, ripening through late summer and fall. Duke is an old Mexican-race avocado selection notable for its cold hardiness, historically used both as a fruiting variety in marginal climates and as rootstock material for grafting less cold-tolerant scions in colder parts of the avocado-growing range. Fruit is small, thin-skinned, and rich-flavored, with the anise-scented leaves typical of the Mexican race, ripening in late summer to fall. Because avocados set fruit more reliably with a cross-pollinator, plant Duke alongside a complementary flowering-type cultivar where space allows. Established Duke trees are among the more cold-hardy avocados available, tolerating brief drops into the low 20s Fahrenheit, though a hard freeze during bloom can still eliminate a season's crop.
